description: The 1989 revolutions, Yeltsin's rise, the August 1991 coup and the end of the Soviet Union.
content_html:
The Revolutions of 1989

When Gorbachev signalled that the Brezhnev Doctrine was dead — that Soviet tanks would no longer prop up unpopular communist governments in Eastern Europe — the result was a cascade of revolutions across the Soviet bloc in 1989. Poland held partly-free elections in June 1989 in which Solidarity swept to power. Hungary opened its borders with Austria, allowing East Germans to escape to the West. In November 1989 the Berlin Wall fell amid scenes of jubilation. Within weeks, communist governments in Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Romania had collapsed. Romania's revolution was the only violent one: the dictator Nicolae Ceauşescu was executed on 25 December 1989.

These revolutions had an electrifying effect on the nationalities within the Soviet Union itself. If Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia could free themselves, why not Ukraine, Estonia, Lithuania or Georgia? Nationalist movements that had been suppressed for decades began to demand independence openly.

Key Fact

In 1989, communist governments fell across Eastern Europe. The Berlin Wall came down in November 1989. These revolutions were made possible by Gorbachev’s refusal to deploy Soviet military force to save them — a decisive break from the Brezhnev Doctrine.

The Baltic States and the Rise of Nationalism

The three Baltic states — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — had been forcibly incorporated into the Soviet Union in 1940 under the terms of the Nazi-Soviet Pact. In 1989 and 1990, all three declared their intention to seek independence. On 23 August 1989, approximately two million people formed a human chain — the “Baltic Way” — stretching from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius, demanding independence on the 50th anniversary of the Nazi-Soviet Pact.

Lithuania declared independence on 11 March 1990 — the first Soviet republic to do so. Gorbachev imposed an economic blockade and sent in troops; a confrontation in Vilnius in January 1991 killed 14 Lithuanian civilians. But the independence movement could not be stopped. By September 1991, all three Baltic states had internationally recognised independence.

Boris Yeltsin had been a Communist Party official who fell out with Gorbachev in 1987 after publicly demanding faster reforms. He was expelled from the Politburo but won election to the Congress of People's Deputies in 1989. In June 1991 he was elected President of the Russian Republic in the first direct democratic election in Russian history — winning 57 per cent of the vote against Communist Party-backed opponents.

Yeltsin's election gave him a democratic mandate that Gorbachev, who had never stood in a direct popular election, lacked. This undermined Gorbachev's authority within the USSR and created a second power centre: a Russian president who could challenge the Soviet president. The two men had a tense, competitive relationship that became central to the final collapse of the USSR.

The August Coup, 1991

On 19 August 1991, a group of senior Soviet officials — including the Vice President, the Defence Minister, the KGB chief and the Prime Minister — staged a coup against Gorbachev while he was on holiday in Crimea. They announced that Gorbachev was ill and that they were taking emergency control. Soviet tanks were deployed in Moscow. The plotters intended to reverse the reforms and restore conservative communist rule.

The coup failed within three days. Boris Yeltsin famously stood on a tank outside the Russian parliament building, urging Russians to resist. Crowds surrounded the parliament to defend it. Crucially, the military refused to follow orders to storm the building. Key units defected to Yeltsin’s side. The coup leaders lost their nerve, the tanks withdrew, and Gorbachev returned to Moscow on 22 August. The August 1991 coup had failed, but it had fatally discredited the Communist Party.

Key Fact

The August 1991 coup failed within three days. Yeltsin’s visible resistance made him the hero of Russian democrats. The failed coup fatally discredited the Communist Party: Gorbachev suspended it on 24 August 1991, and Soviet republics rushed to declare independence.

After the failed coup, Soviet republics declared independence in rapid succession. On 8 December 1991, the leaders of Russia (Yeltsin), Ukraine and Belarus met at Belavezha Forest and signed the Belavezha Accords, declaring that the Soviet Union had “ceased to exist” and creating the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) as a loose successor framework.

On 25 December 1991, Gorbachev resigned as Soviet President and the red Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin, replaced by the Russian tricolour. The USSR formally dissolved on 31 December 1991, splitting into 15 independent states. It was the largest peaceful territorial dissolution of a state in modern history — though not all of the subsequent transitions were peaceful.
exam_tip_html: A common error in questions on the Soviet collapse is to treat it as simply the result of Gorbachev’s reforms. In fact multiple factors converged: the 1989 Eastern European revolutions, nationalist movements within the USSR, Yeltsin’s democratic challenge to Gorbachev, the failed August coup, and the long-term economic crisis. For ‘Explain a Consequence’ questions about the August coup, think about what changed in its immediate aftermath: the party was suspended, republics rushed to declare independence, and Gorbachev’s authority collapsed. For 16-mark essays, weigh which factor was most important in the final collapse.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1989 revolutions across Eastern Europe, made possible by Gorbachev’s abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine, unleashed nationalist movements within the USSR. Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence, in March 1990.
  • Boris Yeltsin was elected President of Russia in June 1991, creating a democratic power centre challenging Gorbachev. The August 1991 coup failed within three days; Yeltsin’s resistance fatally discredited the Communist Party.
  • The Belavezha Accords (8 December 1991) declared the Soviet Union dissolved. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991 and the USSR ceased to exist on 31 December 1991.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the revolutions that swept Eastern Europe in 1989.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: communist governments fell across Eastern Europe without Soviet military intervention; the Berlin Wall was demolished in November 1989; Solidarity won free elections in Poland in June 1989; the revolutions were mostly peaceful except in Romania where Ceauşescu was executed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the failed August 1991 coup against Gorbachev.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: a group of senior officials including the KGB chief and Defence Minister staged the coup; Soviet tanks were deployed in Moscow; Yeltsin stood on a tank outside parliament to urge resistance; the coup collapsed within three days when military units refused to storm the parliament.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 for the Soviet Union.
practice_questions.marks:
Key consequence: the fall of the Berlin Wall demonstrated that Gorbachev would not use military force to save Soviet-backed regimes; this emboldened nationalist movements within the USSR itself; Baltic states, Ukraine and other republics accelerated their independence campaigns, eventually leading to the dissolution of the USSR.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise consequence, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: consequence identified and explained.
Developing: consequence identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point, no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Boris Yeltsin’s election as President of Russia in June 1991 for the collapse of the Soviet Union.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: gave Yeltsin a democratic mandate Gorbachev lacked; created a second power centre challenging Soviet authority; boosted Russian independence from the USSR. Over time: Yeltsin's resistance during the August coup made him the hero of Russian democracy; after the coup, Yeltsin signed the Belavezha Accords dissolving the USSR.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of the Soviet collapse:

“The Soviet Union collapsed because of Gorbachev’s personal failures as a leader, not because of deep structural problems.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: Gorbachev underestimated the destabilising effects of glasnost; perestroika created economic chaos without delivering prosperity; he failed to suppress Baltic independence in 1990-91; he failed to build a coalition with Yeltsin; his personal indecisiveness during the coup allowed it to temporarily succeed.

Disagreement: deep structural problems existed: decades of economic stagnation, military overstretch in Afghanistan, nationalities tensions within a multi-ethnic empire, an uncompetitive economy unable to match the West. These problems predated Gorbachev and no Soviet leader had a credible solution.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was nationalism within the Soviet republics the main reason for the collapse of the USSR in 1991? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

For nationalism: Baltic independence movements; Ukrainian nationalism; the 'Baltic Way' human chain of 1989; Lithuania's March 1990 declaration; after the coup, republics rushed to declare independence; Belavezha Accords signed by republic leaders not Gorbachev.

Alternative factors: economic crisis (stagnation, failed perestroika); impact of the 1989 Eastern European revolutions; the failed August coup discrediting the Communist Party; Gorbachev's reforms creating uncontrolled political forces; Yeltsin's democratic challenge from within Russia.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple factors, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more factors explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

glossary_terms.definition: The barrier dividing East and West Berlin, built in 1961 and demolished by East Germans in November 1989, symbolising the collapse of Soviet-backed communist rule.
The various ethnic and national groups within the Soviet Union, many of which pressed for greater autonomy or independence by the late 1980s.
Former Moscow party chief who became Russia's first democratically elected president in June 1991 and played a pivotal role in defeating the August 1991 coup.
The failed attempt by communist hardliners to remove Gorbachev from power in August 1991, which paradoxically accelerated the Soviet collapse by fatally discrediting the Communist Party.
An agreement signed on 8 December 1991 by the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declaring that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist and establishing the Commonwealth of Independent States.
The loose successor organisation to the Soviet Union, established by the Belavezha Accords in December 1991.
